mathematical_review.defect_confirmed: The old reference to that finite family followed the ball cover of K=Q minus O in 3.1; such a cover has no arbitrary small-volume guarantee, since a constant function permits K=Q. mathematical_review.forward_direction: For null discontinuities each positive oscillation superlevel is compact null and admits a finite small cube cover. Grid control bounds all cells meeting that cover. Compactness of the complement supplies finitely many small-oscillation balls and a sufficiently fine common grid. Its Darboux gap is bounded by the low oscillation times box volume plus twice the function bound times the small exceptional-cell volume, giving integrability in 5.1. This branch is unchanged.
mathematical_review.converse_direction: For each positive integer r and budget eta, choose a Darboux gap below eta/(2r). The sum of volumes of cells with oscillation at least 1/r is then below eta/2. Every superlevel point outside the grid skeleton lies in one such cell; the remaining points lie in finitely many degenerate coordinate rectangles of volume zero. Applying 1.1 to precisely these rectangles gives a finite cube cover below eta. Thus each superlevel is content zero, hence null. The existing rational-enlargement and least-code construction in 4.2 and 6.1 supplies a countable cube cover of their union with the geometric budget, retaining the full choice-free iff.
mathematical_review.boundary_cases: For a constant function the high-cell family is empty, while the zero-volume skeleton can still be covered with arbitrarily small cubes; no cover of the whole Q or complement K is being claimed small. The argument also covers spatial dimension one, in which skeleton pieces are points, and degenerate skeleton rectangles in higher dimensions through 1.1.
mathematical_review.no_new_prerequisite: The necessary finite rectangle-to-cube construction is already proved in 1.1, the superlevel covering in 2.2 and the volume estimate in 1.3. No statement, dependency or choice assumption is changed.

consumers.used_step_excerpt: 2.1 For any continuous $h$ on $K_t$, its zero extensions from $\Omega(t)$ and $K_t$ to a nondegenerate closed interval containing $K_t$ in its interior are bounded and can be discontinuous only at $B_t$. By [F11] they are integrable. Their difference is supported on $B_t$ and bounded in absolute value by a constant times $1_{B_t}$; [F8] gives $\int 1_{B_t}=0$, so [F7] shows their integrals agree. The same argument applies on $\widehat K$ and $\widehat\Omega$. The map image in [F3] is compact Jordan, and [F5] makes $g(\cdot,t)$ and $G(\cdot,t)$ integrable on the compact closures. Change of variables on those closures, followed by the open/closed equalities just proved, gives $I(t)=\int_{\widehat K}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi=\int_{\widehat\Omega}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi$, where $G(\xi,t):=g(A_t(\xi),t)J(\xi,t)$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, F11, step 1.1, algebra]
consumers.review: A continuous function on each compact moving closure has bounded zero extensions to a surrounding nondegenerate box. Away from the moving boundary those extensions are continuous, so all their discontinuities lie in that null boundary. The null-discontinuities-implies-integrable direction therefore supplies exactly the Riemann integrability invoked here. This argument uses Lebesgue criterion steps 1.2, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1 and does not rely on the repaired integrable-implies-null step. Open/closed integral agreement then follows by the separately stated zero-content indicator bound.
